descriptive_title: Grade 1 Mathematics: Algebra (Coding) — Sequential Events and Loops Without Screens (C3.1–C3.2)
subject: Mathematics

curriculum_expectations.C3.1: solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events
curriculum_expectations.C3.2: read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes

unit_overview: A 5-day Grade 1 unit on coding without screens, framed around 'Loop the Loop' — Coda the Coding Robot and Looper the Loop Helper. Day 1 introduces sequential code: a list of step-by-step instructions a robot follows in order. Day 2 introduces loops: 'Repeat 4 times' compresses 4 instructions into 1. Day 3 reads existing code and predicts the outcome. Day 4 alters existing code to change the outcome. Day 5 capstone — child-written code with sequence and loop.
unit_learning_goal: Children will write and execute simple code with sequential steps and loops, read existing code and predict outcomes, and alter code to change the result.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Code is a list of steps in ORDER. The order matters — change the order, and the outcome changes.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can write step-by-step code for a simple task and follow it in order.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Coda introduces sequential code; whole-class 'make a peanut-butter sandwich' code; partner code-and-execute on grid mat.

lesson_arc.big_idea: When we repeat the same step, we can use a LOOP. 'Repeat 4 times: take a step' is shorter than writing 'take a step' four times.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can use a loop in my code to repeat steps.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Looper introduces loops; class chants 'repeat 4 times: clap'; movement code on the grid mat with loops.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We can READ code and predict what it will do BEFORE running it. Predicting tests our understanding.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can read code and predict what will happen when it runs.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Coda hands the class pre-written code; children predict; then execute and check.

lesson_arc.big_idea: When we change code, the outcome changes. We can predict the effect of our changes BEFORE running.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can change code and predict the new outcome.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Children alter pre-written code (change a number, swap two steps) and predict the new outcome before testing.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We can write code to draw a shape, walk a path, or make music. Code is everywhere.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can write my own code to do a task with sequence and loop.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Children invent their own code (draw a square with loops, walk a path) and share with the class.

recurring_characters.name: Coda the Coding Robot
recurring_characters.role: Lead character. A small friendly robot that follows instructions exactly. Anchors all 5 lessons.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A small square robot with a screen face showing emotions, two extending arms, and treads for feet. Yellow body with antenna. Friendly emoticon eyes.

recurring_characters.name: Looper the Loop Helper
recurring_characters.role: Coda's friend. The 'repeat' expert. Anchors Lesson 2 and reappears throughout.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A round robot with a circular spinning antenna. Loop-shaped body design, three small wheels. Encouraging beeps.

threaded_vocabulary.child_friendly_definition: A list of step-by-step instructions for a robot or computer to follow.
A list of steps in ORDER. The first step happens first, then the second, then the third.
A way to repeat the same step many times. 'Repeat 4 times: take a step' is a loop.
To RUN code — follow the steps and do what they say.
To say what you THINK will happen before it happens.
To change. We can ALTER code by adding, removing, or changing steps.

assessment_strategy.diagnostic: Lesson 1: can the child write 3 sequential steps for a simple task (brush teeth, walk to the door)?
assessment_strategy.formative: Lesson 2: can the child use a loop to repeat steps? Lesson 3: can the child predict the outcome of code? Lesson 4: can the child change code and predict the new outcome?
assessment_strategy.summative: Lesson 5 Capstone: child writes their own code with sequence AND loop, executes it correctly.

pedagogical_notes: C3.1+C3.2 are the K-3 coding-without-screens expectations. The 'no screens' caveat means we use grid mats, paper robot tokens, physical movements.
Sequence is foundational: 'first this, then this'. The order matters.
Loops are the first abstraction: a way to compress repetition. Children should see the SHORTER code as a benefit.
Predicting outcomes is metacognitive — it tests understanding before testing on the grid.
Altering code shows that changes have consequences — this is the foundation of debugging.
canadian_context_notes: Canadian classrooms use Scratch Jr or other coding tools, but the curriculum says 'without screens' for early grades.
The grid mat is portable — works in any classroom without computers.
